summary: Follow-up bridge call after the degradation in the attenuation pipeline. Goal was to hand off mitigations, align on hardened runbook, and schedule realistic on-prem load tests. Discussed KV-cache failure modes, transient batching backpressure, VPC/KMS constraints, and customer trust restoration steps.
topics: Next steps: load test scheduling and documentation handoff
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-12-09 14:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Meeting recorded by Fireflies
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Sharma (Redwood SE), Elena Torres (Northstar Head of Platform), Jared Kim (Northstar SRE), Priya Nair (Northstar CISO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. this is Maya from Redwood, and ravi is with me. we wanna make sure we walk through the attenuation pipeline follow-up and handover the hardened runbook.
[00:20] Elena Torres: hey maya, thanks. quick note — we have Priya and Jared on because they're owning the ops and compliance side. uh, we wanna be sure this handoff is concrete.
[00:32] Ravi Sharma: yep. quick recap, from our post-incident analysis the sequence was: elevated small tail requests that triggered prefix cache churn, leading to kv-cache eviction storms and then batching backpressure that cascaded into request timeouts. some of the telemetry showed an odd kernel-selection spike on certain quantized variants.
[01:05] Jared Kim: i, i just wanna stop there — when you say "kv-cache eviction storms" can you explain again? was that because of sequence-length distribution change?
[01:15] Ravi Sharma: right, so the traffic shifted — more long-context calls plus a higher churn of prefixes. our automatic prefix caching couldn't hold the working set, so the kv-store started evicting items, which forced full attention recompute and then batching queue growth. in short, more syncs to disk-ish paths, higher p95.
[01:40] Jared Kim: and that produced the async backlog... yeah that aligns with what we saw — CPU spiking then GPU queuing.
[01:48] Priya Nair: from security, can we confirm if any customer PII was in logs that were shipped to Redwood? we need to be sure about retention and encryption at rest.
[01:59] Maya Chen: good question. short answer: logs we collected were redacted by our collector, but we'll provide the attestation and the specific retention window. we'll also show the KMS integration notes.
[02:12] Elena Torres: the team also flagged that the fallback policy for model variants fired a few times and produced lower-quality responses. that was a customer-visible regression and hit trust.
[02:25] Ravi Sharma: yeah, fallback to the low-cost quantized variant isn't perfect for those long-context prompts. we can tighten the routing policy so that during degraded KV-cache health we route to the warm dedicated pool or a compatible non-quantized variant. that reduces latency variance but costs more.
[02:46] Jared Kim: cost vs latency, the usual. the business asks us to prioritize availability and consistent latencies so we can keep SLAs.
[02:54] Maya Chen: understandable. our proposed triage: 1) short-term control: increase reserved cache size and apply aggressive prefix prefetch for the specific endpoints; 2) mid-term: run a canary that simulates the long-context distribution against the dedicated pool; 3) long-term: add better admission control so batching queues don't exceed X ms per token.
[03:18] Elena Torres: that admission control — who implements it? us or you?
[03:22] Ravi Sharma: Redwood runtime can enforce admission policies for hosted or dedicated. for private deployments, we provide the admission-control module and config example. for your VPC deployment we can send an opinionated config.
[03:36] Priya Nair: and that needs to work with our SSO and RBAC; we use SAML and an in-house IdP. also need audit logs to show who changed policies.
[03:48] Maya Chen: absolutely. our console supports SAML SSO and per-token audit trails. we'll include the audit policy and a sample event stream in the attestation pack.
[03:58] Jared Kim: ok, jumping into the runbook draft you sent — on page 3 there's a step that says "force compact kv-store" — is that safe to run in prod? scares us a little.
[04:10] Ravi Sharma: it's safe if done in a rolling fashion. the runbook spells out constraints and a canary-first approach. the step is only for reclaiming memory when eviction thresholds are reached; we included CLI and API calls. but if you'd prefer, we can change that to a less disruptive approach: instead of force-compact, we throttle incoming queue and trigger prefetch warmers.
[04:31] Elena Torres: we'd prefer the throttle + warmer approach. less risk.
[04:34] Maya Chen: noted — we'll update runbook to default to throttle + warmer and keep force-compact as an escalated action with explicit approval required.
[04:43] Jared Kim: about the kernel-selection spike you mentioned earlier — do we have a reproducible test?
[04:47] Ravi Sharma: we do. the internal bench showed a rare path where quantized kernels used a fallback path that wasn't vectorized for long sequence lengths. that increases CPU and mem-copy time. i'll attach the bench trace and the patch that mitigates the kernel path.
[05:07] Jared Kim: please share the bench. we want to run it in our staging.
[05:11] Maya Chen: we'll share it. also we can provision a small dedicated pool for your staging to run the same workload with identical kernels and scheduling. that helps verify the fix before wider rollout.
[05:24] Priya Nair: compliance — we need to see the SOC2 relevant sections and confirm the KMS/HSM flow for key rotation. do you support HSM-backed keys?
[05:35] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood supports KMS integration and can be configured to use HSM-backed keys in the Private deployment. for hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer-managed keys. we'll include a KMS integration slide deck.
[05:48] Elena Torres: what's the short-term customer-visible mitigation we can apply today to reduce the chance of customer-facing regressions?
[05:55] Ravi Sharma: short-term: 1) pin the model routing to the higher-fidelity variant for the top 8 endpoints; 2) enable prefetch for those endpoints; 3) increase prefix cache allocation for the tenant. These three reduce variance and avoid fallback.
[06:15] Jared Kim: how much will that bump our cost? ballpark?
[06:18] Maya Chen: rough numbers in the spreadsheet — chest-level, expect a 12-18% uplift on token cost for those endpoints, but p95 latency improves significantly. we'll send a clean cost delta in the follow-up.
[06:33] Elena Torres: okay that's acceptable short-term. mid-term we want the on-prem load test you mentioned to validate autoscale and fallback behavior under our traffic shape.
[06:44] Ravi Sharma: suggested plan: a staged load test 1) baseline with current config; 2) stress with long-context distribution and random prefix churn; 3) failure-injection step that simulates slow KV-store responses. each stage has pass/fail criteria in the runbook.
[07:05] Jared Kim: about failure injection — do you provide tooling or do we need a custom script?
[07:08] Ravi Sharma: we have an internal chaos script that simulates latency on the kv layer; we'll sanitize and share it. you can run it in your staging. we'll run it with you during the scheduled load test.
[07:20] Priya Nair: for the audit trail, can you show example events for when a fallback policy toggles or when admission control throttles? we need to be able to correlate to security logs.
[07:31] Maya Chen: yes, the console emits structured events: fallback.toggle, admission.throttle.start/stop, kv.eviction.high. we'll include examples and the mapping to common SIEM fields.
[07:43] Elena Torres: perfect. one more ask — we need an executive one-pager for our leadership that says what happened, what's done, and what remains. keep it non-technical.
[07:54] Maya Chen: we'll produce that. action item: Maya to send exec one-pager and hardened runbook by Friday (2026-12-11).
[08:02] Jared Kim: thanks. on the runbook changes we discussed — default to throttle + warmer, include the bench trace, and the admission policy example.
[08:11] Ravi Sharma: will do. i'll also produce a short checklist for the on-prem engineer that walks through applying the config and running the chaos script.
[08:20] Elena Torres: timeline — we'd like the on-prem load test the week of 2026-12-15. is that feasible?
[08:27] Maya Chen: yes, i'll coordinate availability.
[08:29] Priya Nair: last, re: data retention — please confirm logs we sent were redacted. we need that confirmation in writing.
[08:36] Maya Chen: yes we'll attach the redaction log and retention snapshot to the attestation pack by 2026-12-10.
[08:43] Jared Kim: ok, any blockers from your side, ravi?
[08:46] Ravi Sharma: none, just need the traffic profile and permission to provision a small dedicated staging pool for the test.
[08:53] Elena Torres: we'll send the profile today.
[08:55] Maya Chen: great. quick recap of next steps — we'll send runbook, exec one-pager, bench traces, and KMS integration docs. schedule the on-prem load test for week of Dec 15. red team / compliance attestation by Dec 10.
[09:10] Priya Nair: sounds good. thanks for the clear plan.
[09:14] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email and update the ticket with action items. bye.

End of transcript.
notes: Transcript contains minor transcription errors; speaker tags occasionally generic. Runbook will be updated to prefer throttling+prefetch as default; force-compact retained as escalation. Customer prioritizes availability over minimal cost increases.
